Since the offset was added via `add_offset` in `submit`, the offset now appears processed, and the commit loop will advance `last_committed` past it even though the message was never successfully handled. Any consumer relying on the commit guarantee ("Only commits offsets after successful processing" per the class docstring) will silently lose that message on restart. If at-most-once semantics are intentional, the docstring and metric naming should say so; otherwise failed items need a retry/dead-letter path before the offset is completed.

File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 337, Issue: Commit after terminate: `terminate()` sets `shutdown_event` but never joins `commit_thread`, unlike `close()`. The commit thread waits on `shutdown_event.wait(1.0)` and can wake up one more time after termination, calling `commit_function` concurrently with (or after) the strategy has been torn down. Depending on what `commit_function` does (e.g., producer commit on a closed producer), this can raise or commit offsets at an unsafe point during shutdown.

File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 296, Issue: Assert for control flow: `submit` uses `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` to extract the partition/offset. Under `python -O` asserts are stripped, and `message.value.partition` would then raise `AttributeError` on a non-BrokerValue, which is caught by the broad `except Exception` and silently swallowed (offset never tracked). A explicit check with proper handling would be safer.

findings: File: pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go, Line: 30, Issue: Cache key collision: The new `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the key by naive string concatenation with `_` separators, without escaping or a fixed-length encoding. Since user UIDs, actions, names, and parents can themselves contain underscores, distinct tuples can produce identical keys (e.g., `name="a_b", parent="c"` and `name="a", parent="b_c"` both yield `ns.perm_<user>_<action>_a_b_c`). A cached denial for one resource would then be wrongly returned for another, denying a user access they should have. Using a delimiter that cannot appear in the components (or hashing/encoding the components) avoids this.

File: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go, Line: 116, Issue: Stale denial cache: The new denial cache is checked before the permission cache and is never invalidated or overwritten when access is later granted. Scenario: a user's check is denied at T0, so the denial is cached. An admin then grants the user the permission and the permission cache is refreshed (e.g., via another request that populates `permCache` with allowed=true). Subsequent `Check` calls still short-circuit on the denial cache entry and return `Allowed: false` for the remainder of `shortCacheTTL`, even though fresh permissions allow the action. Since the full-check path (which would set allowed=true) never deletes the denial key, the denial persists independently of the permission cache's own TTL/invalidation. Consider deleting the denial key whenever a check succeeds, or invalidating it on permission changes.

File: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go, Line: 153, Issue: Denial cached on stale data: When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns a cached permission set and `checkPermission` yields allowed=false, the code falls through to the full DB path and re-checks — good. However, if that full path also denies, the denial is written to `permDenialCache` keyed only by namespace/user/action/name/parentFolder. The denial may have been produced from a cached permission snapshot that is itself stale (e.g., permissions were just revoked and later restored within `shortCacheTTL`), extending the effective staleness window beyond the permission cache TTL. This is a lower-severity consistency concern tied to the same invalidation gap as the stale-denial issue.
